newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Krupp sees enough nations meeting EMU goals.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Krupp sees enough nations meeting EMU goals.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Monday that the European Union had made all necessary institutional preparations to allow the planned single currency to be as stable as the mark.

Krupp also said that given success achieved so far in reaching monetary stability among EU members, a sufficient number of nations could be expected to fulfil the inflation, interest rate and exchange rate criteria.
Krupp noted that the Maastricht Treaty did not require exact adherence to the deficit criterion which states that a country's deficit must not exceed three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"Medium-term sustained consolidation is decisive, not an exact fulfilment of the reference level (of the deficit criterion) at the start of the monetary union," Krupp said in the text of the speech.

Economically it made no sense why a deficit of 2.9 percent during an economic boom should be compatible with monetary stability while a figure of 3.2 percent in a recession harboured the threat of inflation, Krupp said.
Krupp also said that the Treaty did not envisage a postponement of the planned January 1, 1999 launch date, adding that a delay made no sense from an economic point of view.

"Rising doubts about the realisation of monetary union could result in a strengthening of the exchange rate of the mark and other stable currencies and lead to further exchange rate-related job losses," Krupp said.

The text of the speech was made available ahead of delivery to an anniversary celebration in Hamburg. Krupp is president of the state central bank of Hamburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Schleswig-Holstein.
Krupp noted that "stability awareness" in Europe had increased, with inflation rates in the EU having fallen to levels which years ago would not have been thought possible.

"In parallel, interest rates have converged at a low level. So financial markets do not share the fear often expressed here (in Germany) that inflation will rise significantly with the launch of monetary union and German investors will suffer corresponding price declines...," he said.
Whether the euro would be stable depended on the implementation of its institutional basis.

"The most important preconditions for a stable euro are fulfilled: the European Central Bank (ECB) is independent, it is committed to prioritising price stability, and there must be no central bank lending to the state."

Economic policymakers, unions and employers had strong incentives to maintain price stability after monetary union since without the possibility of currency depreciation, unjustified wage increases would directly hit competitiveness and curb employment.

In addition, the stability and growth pact ratified at last week's Amsterdam summit of EU leaders envisaged strengthened supervision and coordination of public budgets in EU countries as well as speeding up procedures if a country runs up an excessive deficit, Krupp said.

"So institutionally all preparations have been made with whose help the euro can be as stable as the mark. Of course one must keep working to achieve stability. The Europeans have proven in recent years that they are determined to do so."
Krupp also said the German economy had much to benefit from a single currency.
"Given the size of the euro block, swings of the dollar and the yen against the euro should be smaller than against the mark today."
